**Google Tracks Users Even With Location Services Off, Reveals Report**

**Ad**: Concerned about your privacy online? Stay protected with the latest security apps.

**Body**:  
Google has confirmed it has been able to track the location of Android users by collecting information about the addresses of local mobile phone masts—even when location services were turned off and the sim cards were removed. This revelation, initially reported by Quartz, raises important questions about privacy and the assurances provided to Android users regarding their data.

According to the feature report, starting at the beginning of 2017, Google’s Android system began requesting unique Cell IDs from mobile masts. These identifiers, from any modern Android device, were captured by the phone and routinely sent back to Google, giving the company the theoretical ability to track a device’s location. This could happen even when users believed they had taken appropriate measures to protect their privacy, such as disabling location settings or removing the SIM card altogether.

A spokesperson from Google explained that the company started considering the use of Cell ID codes to improve the speed and reliability of message delivery on the network. However, they emphasized that Cell IDs were never incorporated into Google’s network sync system and that any collected data was immediately discarded. The service was subsequently updated so that Cell IDs were no longer requested from devices.

Further details revealed that alongside Cell IDs, Google also requested the mobile country code and mobile network code—details primarily used to keep devices seamlessly connected to Google’s Firebase Cloud Messaging system. This system handles the delivery of push notifications and messages, maintaining a persistent connection that is essential for services to return data efficiently to users. To reduce battery drain, a process called heartbeat analysis determines the minimum number of connection "pings" required.

Despite Google’s statement regarding the use and disposal of this data, privacy advocates have raised concerns. The ability to triangulate a user’s position using information from multiple cell masts means users can be located within a radius as small as 400 meters—sometimes with even greater accuracy in urban areas. The full implications of this feature remain under scrutiny as users become increasingly aware of how their personal data is collected and utilized by major tech firms.

As technology evolves, it’s important for users to evaluate their privacy settings and understand the full scope of information sharing associated with every service they use. For now, questions remain about how companies like Google handle both the intent and execution of features that may unintentionally overstep privacy boundaries.
